title: The storm and the tombs (Luke 8:22–39)
hook: he stills a storm, then heals a man living among graves
tomorrow: your faith has made you well

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sower and an honest and good heart. Your line was bear fruit with patience. Did you water the stuck thing once more and leave it alone? Day five hundred thirty-two.

"Let us go over unto the other side of the lake." That's all Jesus says. They push off. And he falls asleep in the boat. On a small boat, the mood can change in minutes. Luke says "there came down a storm of wind on the lake." Water pours in. The boat fills. Some of these men are fishermen who know this lake, and they're terrified. And the teacher is still asleep. Two stories follow, back to back, one on the water and one among graves, and they share a single thread: chaos, and then a sudden quiet.
screen: `LET US GO OVER TO THE OTHER SIDE.`
`A STORM CAME DOWN ON THE LAKE.`

segments.voice: They wake him: "Master, master, we perish." And Luke says: "he arose, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: and they ceased, and there was a calm." The Greek for calm is galene, the glassy stillness of the sea after the wind drops. Then he asks: "Where is your faith?" Not a lecture. A question. And now they're afraid in a new way, and full of wonder: "What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him." Then they land on the far shore, in the country of the Gadarenes, where a herd of pigs is feeding on the hillside. A man runs out to meet them who, Luke says, "ware no clothes, neither abode in any house, but in the tombs." Chained and guarded, he broke free again and again. Jesus asks him a plain human question: "What is thy name?" And he answers: "Legion." A legion was a Roman army unit, and Luke explains the name: "many devils were entered into him." He doesn't even have a name of his own anymore, just a crowd. Jesus frees him; the spirits go into the pigs, which rush into the lake. And when the townspeople come, they find the man "sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind." The same quiet as on the lake. The storm inside a person stilled, like the storm on the water. The man begs to go with Jesus. Jesus says no: "Return to thine own house, and shew how great things God hath done unto thee." Go home. And he does, telling the whole city.
screen: then, large: `RETURN TO THINE OWN HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: calm one storm in someone else. Settle, and breathe. First, let your own water go still. Breathe slowly until the surface inside you is a little glassier. Then think of someone in a storm right now: a friend who's panicking, a child who can't sleep, a coworker spinning, a parent who's anxious about everything. Picture yourself with them. You can't command the wind. But you can be the calm one in the boat. A steady voice. A slow sentence. A question: what's your name for this? What's really going on? Imagine sitting with them until something settles. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, simply send them stillness. The bell holds the time.
Galene, the Greek word for a calm, the glassy stillness of the sea when the wind drops: Jesus stills a storm on the lake, then frees a man living among the tombs, and sends him home.

Your line: return to your house. Today, bring calm to one person in a storm, starting at home. And look back at the week: a centurion, a widow, John's question, a woman's tears, diakoneo, good soil, a calm sea. Day five hundred thirty-two, and another week on the path.

screen: `DAY 532 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOUR FAITH HAS MADE YOU WELL.`

howItsDone: Some Christians pray with the stilling of the storm in times of fear, and the healed man sent home to tell his story is sometimes read as a picture of faith shared first with family and neighbors.

original.note: Greek: a calm, the stillness of the sea when the wind drops.

trapdoor: what you thought: two separate miracles.
what it means: a storm on the water and a storm in a man, and in both, Jesus brings a sudden calm.
what a scholar hears: "legion" was a Roman army word, and Luke explains it: many devils had entered him. the man ends the story sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed, in his right mind.

notes: 'Legion' answer quoted in the voice as a single word: 'Legion' (8:30). A Roman legion as 'several thousand soldiers': standard. Confirm.
The region as 'mostly non-Jewish country' is inferred from the herd of pigs and the Decapolis setting. Confirm.

Reviewer edit: 'more frightened now than during the storm' changed to 'afraid in a new way, and full of wonder'; Luke 8:25 says 'being afraid wondered' but does not compare the two fears.
'A storm of wind came down' is KJV 8:23 wording used in the hook; 8:23 is listed among the paraphrase refs. Confirm whether it should get its own quoted source line.
